title: New York City pausing some AI tools in schools
content:
“A six-year-old child is too young to slice an onion, to fry an egg or to use a stove safely. But once that child becomes 16, that knowledge becomes something they are mature enough to learn,” stressed New York’s Mayor Zohran Mamdani, while announcing a one-year moratorium on AI tools for students.
In what has been described as one of “the most expansive student-facing AI policies in the country”, the Mayor and Schools Chancellor Kamar H. Samuels on September 2 imposed a one-year moratorium on student-facing generative AI for pupils up to eighth grade for the 2026–27 academic year.
Here’s what you need to know about the moratorium, why NYC introduced it, and why the move could set a global precedent.
This move will affect nearly 6,00,000 public school students across the United States’ largest school district. Companion chatbots will be prohibited across all grades, while the AI components of more than 38 previously approved programmes that fail to meet the new standards will be disabled or discontinued.
However, not all AI has been banned. Teachers can continue to use approved tools for planning and administrative work. Assistive technologies required by students with disabilities, as well as certain AI tools used in career-readiness programmes, remain permitted where necessary and under the policy’s safeguards.
Five limited AI pilots will also operate throughout the year for high school classrooms. These select tools are Quill (15 minutes per week) for English language arts; Edia (20 minutes per week) for mathematics; Brisk Teaching (10 to 20 minutes once or twice weekly) for teacher-created activities; Playlab (two assignments per marking period; 45 minutes per week) for assignment-specific applications; and Intel AI-Ready Schools (one period per week) to assist students in identifying community issues and developing solutions through term-long projects.
Every high school student will complete two 45-minute modules per year aimed at developing critical thinking around AI use, including its risks, limitations, and scope. Alongside AI restrictions, tighter individual screen-time limits have also been introduced. Children from 2-K through to second grade will have no routine screen time. For those in grades three to five, NYC Public Schools recommends no more than 30 minutes a day of individual screen use; for grades six to eight, the recommendation is 45 minutes. These restrictions do not prohibit teacher-led use of computers, tablets, or interactive whiteboards during lessons.
Throughout the academic year, a panel comprising students, educators, parents, elected officials, union partners, and field experts will assess the impact of the moratorium and pilots, delivering a report with policy recommendations in April 2027.
“Children need teachers and human connection in order to learn and grow,” Mr. Mamdani said. “They need to develop skills alongside their peers, build relationships with educators, and wrestle with tough problems on their own.” Mr. Samuels also made a similar argument. Learning, he said, involves getting something wrong, trying again and eventually getting it right. That struggle is not an inconvenience that technology should eliminate; it is part of the learning process.
This move arrives amidst growing concern over screen time harming youth mental health. Studies have linked excessive scrolling, social media exposure and reliance on AI in children to lower critical thinking abilities, shorter attention spans, anxiety, and depression. While evidence connecting AI chatbots to suicide risk remains limited, several cases have prompted lawsuits alleging that interactions with chatbots contributed to young people’s deaths. Mr. Mamdani’s decision follows OpenAI’s launch of a teenage version of ChatGPT on August 18 featuring parental controls and content restrictions regarding self-harm and suicide. On August 26, Meta similarly announced stricter time limits, night-time blocking, and muted notifications during school hours for teenage accounts on Instagram and Facebook.
“The tech industry wants us to believe that AI-powered early education is not only inevitable but necessary. We do not see it that way,” Mr. Mamdani added.
Research supports a cautious stance. A 2026 CEPR discussion paper by researchers at Stockholm University and the University of Hong Kong examined more than 26,000 students in China over 30 months. They found that access to generative AI increased homework scores by 18% and reduced completion time by 30%. However, after roughly six months, the same students’ closed-book examination scores had fallen by 20%. A broader review by the Brookings Institution’s Centre for Universal Education, analysing over 400 studies and interviews with 500 educators and pupils across 50 countries, concluded that the potential harms of generative AI in primary and secondary education currently outweigh the benefits—though tailored applications with proper safeguards can enrich learning.
How are other parts of the world dealing with a similar dilemma? The United Arab Emirates is moving towards more structured AI education, rather than a moratorium. It has announced an AI curriculum across public and private schools covering areas such as data, algorithms, applications, risks and ethical use. It also plans to train about 22,000 educators in using AI for teaching, assessment, curriculum analysis and lesson planning.
Norway has adopted a more cautious approach. Its education authorities have recommended that pupils in grades one to seven should not be given access to generative AI, while students in eight to 10 should be introduced to it gradually.
Australia has taken another route: a national framework for responsible and ethical use of generative AI in schools, rather than a blanket prohibition. The European Union, meanwhile, has sought to regulate high-risk uses of AI. Under the EU AI Act, certain systems used in education — including those involved in evaluating learning outcomes or determining access to education — can fall into the high-risk category. The legislation does not amount to a general ban on generative AI in schools.
Poland is going further in the opposite direction, investing almost 1.9 billion zloty to equip 12,000 schools with AI laboratory sets as part of its broader digital education push.
And where does India stand? India is closer to the integration camp. The National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 identifies artificial intelligence and other emerging technologies as important to India’s changing educational and employment landscape, and calls for contemporary subjects such as AI to be introduced at appropriate stages, alongside greater emphasis on computational thinking.
The Central Board of Secondary Education (CBSE) introduced Artificial Intelligence as an optional sixth subject in Class IX from the 2019-20 academic session. More recently, for 2026-27, CBSE launched a dedicated Computational Thinking and Artificial Intelligence curriculum for Classes III to VIII, with AI and allied-subject curricula for Classes IX to XII also finalised. The curriculum emphasises logical reasoning, pattern recognition, algorithm design, data literacy and responsible and ethical AI use.

report.summary: NYC imposes one-year moratorium on student-facing generative AI through eighth grade, with limited pilots, citing developmental risks.
report.background: New York City’s public school system, the largest in the U.S., announced a one-year pause on generative AI tools used directly by students from September 2026 through the 2026–27 academic year. Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Schools Chancellor Kamar H. Samuels framed the move as protecting childhood development, arguing that children need struggle, human connection, and age-appropriate skills before encountering AI. The policy affects roughly 600,000 students, prohibits companion chatbots across all grades, and disables AI features in 38 previously approved programmes that do not meet new standards. It follows growing parental and scientific concern about screen time, mental health, critical thinking, and chatbot-related risks. The decision arrives shortly after OpenAI released a teen-focused ChatGPT and Meta tightened teen account restrictions, reflecting broader anxiety about youth exposure. NYC will evaluate the moratorium through pilots and a panel report due April 2027.
key_points: The moratorium covers student-facing generative AI up to eighth grade across NYC’s public schools, affecting around 600,000 students. Companion chatbots are banned for all grades, and AI features in existing approved programmes will be disabled if they fail new safeguards.

Teachers may still use AI for planning and administration, and assistive technologies for disabled students are exempt. Five limited high-school pilots—Quill, Edia, Brisk Teaching, Playlab, and Intel AI-Ready Schools—will operate under strict time caps and oversight.

Screen-time limits accompany the AI pause: children from 2-K through second grade get no routine individual screen time, while grades 3–5 and 6–8 are recommended at most 30 and 45 minutes daily respectively, excluding teacher-led device use.

Research cited by officials shows mixed outcomes. A CEPR study of 26,000 Chinese students found AI raised homework scores 18% but later cut closed-book exam scores by 20%; Brookings concluded harms of generative AI in K-12 education currently outweigh benefits without tailored safeguards.
report.impact: NYC’s pause signals a major policy shift for U.S. school districts and may influence other jurisdictions weighing AI adoption. It recognises AI’s potential in administration and carefully controlled assignments while prioritising child development, critical thinking, and mental health. For the AI industry, the moratorium creates friction for vendors selling directly to younger students in the largest U.S. district, potentially pushing them toward teacher-facing tools, compliance features, and age-gated safeguards. Developers may need to adjust product designs to meet stricter standards around screen time, assessment integrity, and data ethics. For regular users and families, this underscores the need for evidence-based evaluation rather than edtech hype. The April 2027 report will be closely watched globally; if successful, similar precautionary policies may emerge, especially amid mixed international approaches from the UAE’s structured curricula to Poland’s heavy AI investment.
report.tools: Educators and policymakers can follow the pilots: Quill for writing, Edia for math, Brisk Teaching for teacher workflows, Playlab for assignment design, and Intel AI-Ready Schools for project-based learning. Researchers may explore NYC’s April 2027 evaluation, CEPR working papers, and Brookings’ AI in education reviews. Open-source alternatives like Moodle with AI plugins, LangChain-based tutor prototypes, or Khanmigo’s public research summaries can help compare safe, teacher-led AI integration.
